title: Historic Sonoma Barn With Modern Amenities Hits the Market
summary:
The Sonoma estate, salvaged from an 1840s New Jersey barn, retains its antique charm while providing modern touches.

The post Historic Sonoma Barn With Modern Amenities Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A barn-turned-residence on 2.8 acres in Sonoma is currently listed for sale. With three bedrooms, three bathrooms and a combined 4,450 square feet of living space, the main home and detached guesthouse are priced at $4,950,000.

The historic barn — located on an open meadow with views of Sonoma Mountain — had a previous life in Neshanic, New Jersey. In 2007, designer Barbara Johnsen arranged for a circa-1840 barn to be salvaged and moved across the country. 

Johnsen tapped Santa Rosa architect Sara Woodfield to convert the antique structure into a home. The silo, added to enclose a circular staircase, provides an on-theme focal point. A weathervane-topped cupola skylight illuminates the great room while adding to the barn’s unique, cinematic presence.

The structure maintains its original rough-hewn and weight-bearing barn frame. Exposed-wood trusses crown the space with historic charm while the white walls and numerous French doors create an airiness.

The home has been updated with modern amenities including high-speed internet, integrated AV, Sonos audio and solar. Current homeowners collaborated with furniture maker Josh Podoll and interior architect Karyn Gabriel to transform the interiors.

Finishes are modern and luxe, from dramatically proportioned marble pieces to walnut floors. Contemporary light fixtures, rich-toned millwork and select deep-toned walls add drama and a pleasing transitional quality to the scheme.

Some of the barn’s original floors were installed by the property’s current listing agent, Matt Sevenau, who owned a flooring showroom in Sonoma before parlaying his home knowledge into a real estate career. Sevenau appreciates the “full-circle” experience of listing the property he witnessed transform 20 years ago.

The grounds include a seasonal creek, olive and fruit trees, raised beds, a bocce court and a sunset porch. The pool receives early evening sunlight.

Sevenau said for the right person, the barn would be like winning the lottery, as there are no other properties like it in Sonoma.

For more information on this property at 21831 Schellville Road in Sonoma, contact listing agents Matt Sevenau, 707-934-5630, Compass, 591 Broadway, Sonoma; or Erin Lial, 707-333-5596, Coldwell Banker, 1200 Main St., St. Helena. dospalmassonoma.com

title: These Sonoma County Wineries Are Farming for the Future
summary:
As new Sonoma County wineries make strides toward sustainability, they join others who have pushed the region forward for decades.

The post These Sonoma County Wineries Are Farming for the Future appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Vance Rose reaches out and plucks a few leaves off a tall, twisting bay laurel tree. I lift them to my nose and smell the powerful, herbaceous aroma. “I love bay laurel,” he says. “It is so lovely.”

A bay laurel tree might not seem to have much to do with wine, but as we hop in a golf cart and drive around Harper’s Rest, a new winery in Russian River Valley named for Reuben Harper, the farmer who originally tended this land in the 19th century, it quickly becomes clear that Rose sees the property not just as a vineyard, but as a holistic, living organism.

He points out the cover crops growing from the untilled soil between the vine rows, the beehives next to the pond, the chicken coop laden with fresh eggs, the garden where he grows produce for the culinary program, the lichen-coated boulders around the tasting room.

Harper’s Rest debuted last year after Young’s Holdings CEO Chris Underwood bought the Healdsburg estate (formerly Arista Winery) and is establishing itself as a standard bearer for sustainability. Rose is not only its winemaker, but its chief apostle for regenerative farming. As we sip Pinot Noir and Chardonnay at an oak-shaded table outside the tasting room, he explains why.

“Organic is pretty straightforward,” he says. “You can’t kill bugs, you can’t kill weeds, and you can’t kill mold with a synthetic, but you can do any of those three things with organic material. Regenerative, you have to be certified organic, but you cannot use even organic herbicide. You can’t kill any weeds, and you can’t till.” One reason, Rose explains, is that microbes aerate soil and provide nutrition to vines. Sprays — even organic ones — and tilling kill those microbes.

The vineyards on the estate around us are still in the certification process, but the winery’s Moon Dust Vineyard, on a plot outside Sebastopol, is already Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC). Rose tells an anecdote from the brutal heat wave during the 2022 harvest, when temperatures soared to 113 degrees, that provides evidence of the impact: “We have a neighbor who grows grapes, he tills, and we took our soil temperature, and we took his less than 20 yards away. Our soil, with this permanent cover crop, was 34 degrees colder than his.” Rose says elevated soil temperatures can stop ripening and cause vine roots to strangle. “We came through 113.2 degrees, not a problem in the world,” he concludes. “He had serious issues.”

Conscientious farming is just one way in which Sonoma County vintners are pushing the envelope when it comes to sustainability. Later that afternoon, I’m on the terrace at Skipstone, another winery that looks out across a California Certified Organic Farmers (CCOF)-certified vineyard in Alexander Valley. General manager Patricia Smith and I turn our gaze from the terraced vines to the winery’s new stone building, which she believes is on its way to being certified LEED Platinum, the highest rating granted by the U.S. Green Building Council, an accomplishment only one other winery in the county — Silver Oak, also in Alexander Valley — has managed. Skipstone’s facility is cut deep into the hillside, reducing the energy needed to cool the solar-powered building, and is constructed of reclaimed redwood and stone quarried on the property.

“One of the things [USGBC assessors] really want to make sure of is building materials and where they’re coming from,” Smith explains. “So, using materials that we’re not flying over from France or Italy, but having stuff that, literally, we dug it up over there, we cracked it, and then we placed it here.” She points to a dark patch in the facade, indicative of volcanic rock, and adds, “It’s also kind of cool, you can see our terroir in the wall.”

While Harper’s Rest and Skipstone may be new leaders in sustainability, there are many local pioneers who have spent decades blazing that trail. Duff Bevill of Bevill Vineyard Management, who began his career in Dry Creek Valley in 1973, remembers working under Joe Vogensen, who was already practicing no-till farming.

“He was the only guy in the valley to do it,” Bevill says. “And when I went on my own, I incorporated something similar. It was hard for me to convince my clients. The first one was Dave Stare at Dry Creek Vineyard, and he thought we were doing something wrong. I said, ‘No, it’s good for the soil.’”

In those days, the concept of organic farming existed, but Bevill says that the main focus was pesticides. Like Rose, he points out that “you still use pesticides. Back then, the emphasis was primarily on whether it was chemical-free or chemical-reduced.”

By the year 2000, sustainability had become a buzzword, and the Sonoma County Grape Growers Association (now Sonoma County Winegrowers, or SCW) began a framework for its members. The initial program was a self-assessment that had been developed by the Lodi-Woodbridge Winegrape Commission, and which vintners could use to judge themselves environmentally, socially, and economically. “You could get into becoming an organic farm model within the sustainability system, but it had so many other categories that were valuable to assess as a grower,” Bevill says. “Are we polluting the air? Are we good to our employees? Are we good to our community? That’s all part of that program.”

The nature of a self-assessed program led to accusations of greenwashing, so the SCW later moved toward using third-party evaluators. According to SCW CEO Karissa Kruse, a qualifying certification can come from the California Sustainable Winegrowing Alliance, the Lodi Rules, Sustainability in Practice (SIP), or Fish Friendly Farming. In 2014, the organization made a commitment to have 100% of its vineyards certified sustainable within five years. Today, the number stands at 99%.

A common critique is that the stringency of the requirements varies based on the organization. “I work with all sorts of different people,” Rose says. “They all say, ‘Oh yeah, I’m on the Sonoma County sustainable thing.’ I’m like, ‘You’re spraying chemicals. That is not sustainable.’ That standard is way too low.” So, many wineries seek to go further, getting certified organic by CCOF, regenerative by the Regenerative Organic Alliance (ROA), or biodynamic by the Demeter Association.

Biodynamics, conceived by Austrian philosopher Rudolf Steiner in the 1920s, shares many tenets with the regenerative framework, looking at a farm as a fully integrated organism that includes soil, plants, and animals. It also incorporates some mystical elements — emphasizing phases of the moon and burying cow horns stuffed with humus and manure. Benziger Family Winery on Sonoma Mountain began converting to biodynamic farming in 1993 and was the first winery in the county to earn a Demeter certification in 2000. Vintner Chris Benziger says he doesn’t necessarily buy into the spiritual aspects of the system, but he’s a true believer in the practical impacts.

“I grew up in the city, and coming out here, there’s all these critters I’ve never seen before — wild turkeys, jackrabbits, bobcats, foxes,” Benziger recalls of the early years on his property in the ’80s and early ’90s when his family was still using commercial pest and weed management chemicals. “Once we would spray, you wouldn’t see any of those critters. By the fourth year, it was silent. And I noticed that the soil was almost changing colors. This soil that had been knitted together with billions of microorganisms was being killed. Here we were professing that we found this gorgeous piece of property that we absolutely loved, yet we were farming it in a way that felt irresponsible.” Today, Benziger not only farms biodynamically, but also offers tractor tours on which interested guests can learn about it.

Visitors to Littorai, outside Sebastopol, also get a lesson in biodynamics during estate tours past compost piles and a shed where the crew prepares teas using native plants to enrich the soil. Littorai winemaker Ted Lemon spent his early career in France. “The 1980s in Burgundy was really the height of conventional farming,” he says. “That’s what I was kind of raised in. I just got to the point where I felt like I was the hamster in its cage going around and around on its exercise wheel. You could go faster and faster, and Western agronomy would ask for more and more inputs.” He studied a variety of agroecological approaches, and he and his wife, Heidi, settled on biodynamics when they bought the Littorai estate in 2000.

Unlike Benziger, Lemon gets into the metaphysical side of the system. “It’s a form of spiritual agriculture,” he says. “It’s the belief that the spiritual world exists, and it manifests itself in all things around us.” He acknowledges that it sounds a bit woo-woo, and admits he was skeptical at first, but the effects of biodynamics — not tilling, promoting cover crop diversity — were undeniable. “I remember in 2009, a year where the first rain of any significance was enormous,” he says, “and I walked out to the bottom of the Pivot Vineyard, and there was no erosion. There were no little rivulets of dirt or anything. It’s like, ‘Oh my goodness, this is really working.’” As for the wine, he adds, “When you look at the measures of a juice panel of grapes, of the nutrient status for the yeast, they’re highest in the biodynamic vineyards.”

While Lemon’s estate would qualify for just about any sustainability certification, he hasn’t pursued any of them. “Anybody who wants to criticize us for that, I totally accept the criticism,” he says. “And people who do the work to get a certification deserve their certification. All I care about is the work on the ground.”

A big hurdle for sustainable farming, given the wine industry’s current downturn, is the expense. Lemon estimates he spends about $1,000 more per acre; Benziger ballparks his costs at around 10% higher. Rose recalls it costing about 6% more per ton to farm organically, and more still for regenerative, in part because labor costs are higher (both because there’s more manual labor involved and because the ROA requires better pay for workers). But cost to him is irrelevant. “I would be organic if it were 50% more expensive,” he says, “because I don’t want to drink that shit.”

Benziger points out that the gap shrinks over time. “They always talk about the initial farming costs, and they are more expensive, but you get better quality wine, and hopefully you can charge more,” he says. He also points out that the typical lifespan of a grapevine is 20 to 25 years, whereas his are 35 to 40 years old. “We’re getting an extra lifespan. And after planting a vineyard, what’s the most expensive thing you can do? Replant. That’s $40,000, probably more now, an acre.”

Even taking the long view, the economic situation for many farmers is bleak. “Agriculture is hurting more than it’s hurt since the Great Depression,” says Carlo Mondavi, who makes Sonoma Coast wines at RAEN Winery. “I’m not just talking about viticulture; I’m talking about corn and soy and veggies, all of it. It’s very difficult to be preachy and tell someone not to do something when they can barely put food on their family’s table.”

Still, this perspective hasn’t stopped Mondavi, the grandson of Napa legend Robert Mondavi, from believing sustainability is paramount. He saw firsthand the impact of chemical inputs when he was just 24, after his family sold Robert Mondavi Winery in 2004.

“We lived on a ranch, and there was a vineyard that separated my grandfather and my father’s house,” he says. The first year after the sale to Constellation Brands, he noticed the grass beneath the vines was turning yellow and orange. “I pulled [my father] outside, and he said, ‘Oh, they’re chemically mowing.’ And I was like, ‘Why would you spray a chemical by the root ball of a plant that you’re trying to grow? Wouldn’t it hurt the plant?’ And the dirt I was standing on was directly above the well where my father and my grandfather split the drinking water, and I said, ‘Wouldn’t we end up drinking this?’”

Mondavi later discovered that coastal California’s monarch butterfly population had decreased by more than 95% since the commercial introduction of Roundup, so in 2016, he issued the Monarch Challenge, calling for farmers to stop using these chemicals. He also became the chief farming officer at Monarch Tractor, which produced autonomous, electric tractors to help cut emissions.

Despite a promising start, Monarch Tractor ceased operations at the beginning of this year, but that setback doesn’t indicate a dead end. Sonoma County Winegrowers has partnered with companies such as John Deere on a “Farm of the Future” project to explore technological advancements. “I think, as we go forward, we’re going to start to be looked at as not only a sustainability leader, but an innovation leader,” says Tyler Klick, co-owner of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management and chair of the SCW board of directors.

Mondavi sounds a similarly optimistic note. “The technology’s arriving at the same time as consumer knowledge and desire are meeting,” he says. “I think that Sonoma will be one of the first fully organic wine regions in the world. When you look more particularly on the West Sonoma Coast, we’re already basically there. [We’re] far ahead of almost any other region in the United States that I know of, which is pretty exciting.”

The post These Sonoma County Wineries Are Farming for the Future appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro Sold After 24 Years to Owners of Lo & Behold
summary:
The owners of a popular Healdsburg cocktail bar and restaurant will take the reins of the west county institution. But don't expect anything to radically change.

The post Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro Sold After 24 Years to Owners of Lo & Behold appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
After nearly 24 years of steak frites, chou-fleur and Hemingways, Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro is changing hands. The good news for its loyal customers: Three of the restaurant’s biggest fans are taking over.

Matthew Greenbaum, who opened the beloved west county restaurant in December 2002, has sold Underwood to Sean Kelley, Tara Heffernon and Laura Sanfilippo, the trio behind Healdsburg’s popular Lo & Behold Bar + Kitchen.

Kelley started as a line cook at Underwood in 2004 and worked his way up to sous chef and co-manager over 12 years. He’s stayed close to Greenbaum ever since and isn’t about to fix what isn’t broken.

“This place is a legacy restaurant with a loyal following. We just want to breathe a little new life into it,” Kelley said.

He knows every nook and cranny of the restaurant, and Greenbaum had joked for years that Kelley should buy it someday. Now, he’s finally taking him up on the offer. Greenbaum’s last official day will be New Year’s Eve.

“I’ve been thinking about it for some time. I’m ready to free up some of my time, and my brain space, to move on to my third act,” said Greenbaum, 65.

That means more time for poetry, travel, creativity and his letterpress studio. But he’s quick to note he’s not heading for a rocking chair anytime soon.

Greenbaum will continue operating Willow Wood Market Cafe, the casual restaurant he opened across the street in 1995. Longtime Underwood general manager Jen Warfel will move there as well.

“Success for me is a new relationship with time,” he said.

That means fewer daily headaches from running a restaurant. And more time for whatever comes next.

A new era

When Greenbaum arrived in the sleepy, apple-processing town in the early 1990s, Graton had a couple of dive bars and plenty of empty buildings. Hitching posts for horses still lined the sidewalks.

Underwood, with its dark interior, red banquettes, nickel bar and Parisian bistro tiles, was an unlikely attraction in the tiny hamlet. It quickly became a gathering place for local winemakers, restaurant workers and neighbors drawn to Greenbaum’s classic French brasserie cooking and the cocktails.

Together, Willow Wood and Underwood helped turn quiet Graton into a dining destination.

“Everything about Underwood I built, designed, and it’s my baby,” he said. “The thought of selling it was hard.”

Finding the right people to take over made the decision easier.

“They understand Underwood well,” he said. “They don’t want to rewrite the script.”

Kelley, Heffernon and Sanfilippo opened Lo & Behold in 2022, building a loyal following for its inventive cocktails, globally inspired comfort food and lively, unpretentious atmosphere.

Heffernon and Sanfilippo were part of the founding team at Duke’s Spirited Cocktails, alongside Cappy Sorentino and Steven Maduro, in 2016. The bar became known for incorporating backyard botanicals into its drinks, helping fuel a craft cocktail movement that has since become commonplace.

The two left Duke’s in 2021 and later joined forces with Kelley, who had run the food program at Burdock, to open Lo & Behold.

“Underwood is a magical place to all three of us. We’re aware of how special a place it is to share a meal and memory,” Sanfilippo said.

The trio hopes to preserve what customers love about Underwood while adding a few touches of their own.

Kelley plans to lean into the restaurant’s original French brasserie roots, with a nod to classic San Francisco dishes such as cioppino. Steak frites and chou-fleur will stay, as will cocktails rooted in the classics.

The biggest changes will include online reservations, a reimagined happy hour and the return of lunch service. Heffernon and Sanfilippo will split their time between Healdsburg and Graton, while Kelley oversees the kitchen transition. Current chef Mark Miller will stay on.

For Greenbaum, the handoff is as much about the people as the place. Finding owners who would look after Underwood’s longtime employees and loyal customers was a priority. He’s confident he’s found them.

He also doesn’t plan to be a stranger.

“I feel like Underwood is going to stay and be there another 25 years,” Greenbaum said, “and I’ll be sitting there having a cocktail.”

title: Rhône-Style Wines and 360-Degree Views Set the Stage at Trattore Farms in Geyserville
summary:
From seasonal paninis and panoramic patio views to ATV tours and estate olive oil tastings, Trattore Farms offers an elevated Wine Country experience in Geyserville.

The post Rhône-Style Wines and 360-Degree Views Set the Stage at Trattore Farms in Geyserville appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Lots of Silicon Valley tech entrepreneurs get bitten by the wine bug. But in Tim Bucher’s case, it was the other way around. Bucher is a wine guy who got bitten by the tech bug.

Raised on his family’s Dry Creek Valley dairy farm, Bucher grew up around legendary winemaking families like the Gallos and Seghesios. While kids his age collected baseball cards, Bucher became fascinated with grapes and wine. At 16, he began growing wine grapes on a 2-acre property he bought with his siblings.

While studying agriculture at UC Davis, Bucher says he “accidentally” switched to computer and electrical engineering. He continued that path at Stanford University and later worked in the technology industry for firms such as Apple and Microsoft.

Despite Bucher’s success in the tech world, farming kept calling him back to Sonoma County. In 1998, he and his wife Mary Louise bought a 40-acre property in Dry Creek Valley and planted it with grapevines and olive trees.

After years of development, the couple launched Dry Creek Olive Co. in the early 2000s, producing estate olive oils and vinegars. They released their first Trattore Farms wines in 2004, naming the winery after the Italian word for tractor. They opened their hilltop winery facility in 2015.

Bucher’s agriculture and technology worlds eventually merged when he grew concerned about rising farm labor costs and regulations. To ease the pressure, Bucher created automated systems for Trattore Farms, including remote-controlled irrigation systems and an autonomous tractor equipped with electric motors, cameras and computers.

At the urging of his Silicon Valley friends, he turned those innovations into a company called Agtonomy. The AI and software services firm helps wineries and farms turn standard tractors and other industrial equipment into autonomous, remotely controlled machinery.

Today, Trattore Farms and Winery sustainably farms 22 varieties of wine grapes and 20 types of olives, using practices such as no-till farming, water recycling and soil-enhancing compost made from grape and olive pomace.

Focusing on Rhône varieties and Zinfandel, winemaker Craig Strehlow produces about 4,500 cases per year.

The vibe

Set amid steep slopes carpeted with vineyards and olive groves, Trattore’s Mediterranean-inspired hilltop winery near Geyserville is 400 feet above the valley floor. The tasting room doubles as a tractor showroom, with various models displayed among bottles of estate olive oils, vinegars and cute ceramic dishes.

As cool as the tractors are, the real show is out on the veranda. There, 360-degree views of Dry Creek Valley mesmerize tasters seated on the expansive patio. The tasting room also offers plenty of bar and table seating for rainy-day visits.

On the palate

Bubbles are always a great place to start, especially when the offering is as intriguing as the 2025 Bolle de Trattore ($58). Aromatic and peachy, with apple notes, the wine combines Picpoul and Viognier.

For a medium-bodied red with strawberry and tobacco spice aromas and ripe raspberry flavor, try the lively 2022 Dry Creek Valley Estate Grenache ($44). The 2022 Dry Creek Valley Proprietor’s Reserve GSM ($60) draws you in with perfumed aromas, then seals the deal with notes of red fruits and spice.

Wine tastings range from $30 for a discovery sampling to $45 for a flight paired with small bites. Olive oil and vinegar tastings cost $30 and include warm bread for dipping. Visitors can also order wines by the glass ($15-$20) and mocktails ($20 per flight or $10 per glass).

For the full experience, the Get Your Boots Dirty Tour ($125) includes an ATV excursion through the property’s rolling hills, stopping along the way to learn about Trattore’s vines and olive trees — one is nearly two centuries old and still producing fruit. You’ll also visit the olive mill to learn how a 4-ton stone mill transforms olives into luscious oils. The experience finishes with a tasting of wines, olive oils and vinegars.

Beyond the bottle

If you find yourself wanting to linger after your tasting, why not stay for lunch? Along with snacks such as seasoned nuts, Trattore Farms offers charcuterie boards, seasonal panini and entrée salads dressed with housemade olive oils and vinegars. You can also order “barcuterie” for your furry friend. Check the website for wood-fired pizza days.

Trattore Farms and Winery, 7878 Dry Creek Road, Geyserville. Open from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Thursday through Monday. 707-431-7200, trattorefarms.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Instagram @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: European-Style Villa in Santa Rosa Hits the Market
summary:
The Sonoma Mountain home in Santa Rosa features unique architectural details from around the world along with a pool, spa and guest cottage.

The post European-Style Villa in Santa Rosa Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A European-style home on 11.65 acres on Sonoma Mountain is currently listed for sale. The three-bedroom, three-bathroom home with a cottage, gardens and pool is priced at $3,775,000.

The main home, built in 2006, is traditionally styled with a stucco exterior, a rounded tower, turning stairways and a clay tile roof. Grapevines climb the dwelling in classic Mediterranean fashion.  

The interior is punctuated with unique architectural details and finishes, many of which are sourced from around the world. Traditional elements include ochre plaster walls, high ceilings and exposed wood beams. Colorful tile, Rondel windows, turned columns and repurposed oversized doors enliven the space. Showstopping arched windows and balconies with intricate ironwork yield to the stunning valley views.

The great room is grandly designed with columns, arches and a Rumford fireplace. The kitchen area has Caesarstone countertops, rustic cabinetry and a reclaimed door in a distressed blue. 

The grounds include stone terraces and stone paths that lead to gardens with flowering arbors and fruit trees. Covered decks include automatic screens and spots for lounging and dining. The pool, spa, dining areas and guesthouse enjoy panoramic views of the Mayacamas mountains.

For more information on this property at 6640 Sonoma Mountain Road in Santa Rosa, contact listing agents Tina Shone, 707-799-7556, or Evan Shone, 707-328-9288, 707-933-1515; Sotheby’s International Realty – Wine Country – Sonoma Brokerage, 793 Broadway, Sonoma. sothebysrealty.com/eng/sales/detail/180-l-1188-gt768e/6640-sonoma-mountain-road-santa-rosa-ca-95404

title: 25 Sonoma County Restaurants for Delicious Plant-Based Meals
summary:
These local restaurants serve excellent plant-based dishes, from meatless comfort food to upscale, farm-to-table bites.

The post 25 Sonoma County Restaurants for Delicious Plant-Based Meals appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County has long been known for its food, from farm-driven California cooking to international specialties and comfort classics. Vegetarian and vegan diners, however, haven’t always had the same range of choices as those who eat meat. That is beginning to change.

Over the past several years, plant-based products have become increasingly common in grocery stores and restaurants nationwide. Sonoma County has followed the trend. Some restaurants have added substantial vegetarian and vegan selections to their menus; others have built their businesses around plant-based cooking.

For those seeking to eat less meat, or simply try something different, here are restaurants across Sonoma County worth visiting on World Vegan Day, Nov. 1, and throughout the year.

Santa Rosa

The Branch Line

Kim Bourdet, who previously owned and operated organic cafe and catering business ​​The Pharmacy, opened this plant-based eatery and mercantile in the former Flying Goat Coffee space in Old Railroad Square in early 2022. Start your day with a seasonal latte, paired with fluffy focaccia, fresh muffins and other pastries. Or go for the bagels with avocado or vegan cream cheese. For lunch on the go, there are salads, sandwiches and grain bowls. Locally made goods to take home include syrups, jams, sauces and dry pasta. 10 Fourth St., Suite 1, Santa Rosa, 707-595-1941, instagram.com/thebranchline_sonomacounty

East West Cafe

A Mediterranean staple for more than 30 years, East West Cafe has a dedicated vegetarian section on its menu. The Mediterranean Platter is a meatless sampler of hummus, falafel, tabbouleh and baba ghanoush. The Macro Plate is a more substantial vegan option, with braised tofu or a vegetable patty, steamed vegetables, hummus, brown rice, oil-free black beans and blue corn tortillas. The Thai Tofu Salad combines marinated tofu with mixed greens, red cabbage, onion, avocado, beets, carrots, toasted almonds and mandarin orange slices, finished with housemade citrus dressing. 557 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa, 707-546-6142, eastwestcafesantarosa.com

The Spinster Sisters

Named the best farm-to-table restaurant in Sonoma County in The Press Democrat’s 2025 Readers’ Choice awards, The Spinster Sisters builds its menu around seasonal produce and farm-fresh ingredients, which can be paired with natural wines in a casual setting. The menu changes regularly, but recent offerings have included Rancho Gordo bean tostadas at weekend brunch, crookneck squash soup with herb pesto and ricotta gnocchi with heirloom cherry tomatoes at dinner. For dessert, a nectarine-brown sugar bread pudding has been among the standouts. 401 South A St., Santa Rosa, 707-528-7100, thespinstersisters.com

Cotati

Lady Blume Microbakery + Coffee

Opened in spring 2024, Lady Blume specializes in gluten- and dairy-free baking. Its plant-based offerings include walnut banana bread, chocolate pound cake, chocolate doughnuts, cornmeal berry muffins and walnut chocolate chip cookies. Dairy-free doughnuts rotate through different flavors, so it’s worth checking the pastry case regularly. 8059 La Plaza, Cotati, ladyblume.com

Petaluma

Aqus Café

This cafe at Foundry Wharf offers several vegan alternatives alongside its traditional menu. Breakfast options include the Veganrito, a burrito filled with rice, potatoes, avocado, cilantro, black beans, red peppers and plant-based mozzarella. At lunch and dinner, the selection expands to vegan and vegetarian wraps, paninis and sandwiches. The Veggie Friday panini combines roasted asparagus, eggplant, sweet peppers, and portobello mushrooms with goat cheese or plant-based mozzarella and sun-dried tomato spread. Other choices include a tempeh Reuben, garden burgers, vegetarian lasagna, and a teriyaki tempeh bowl with brown rice and vegetables. 189 H St., Petaluma, 707-778-6060, aquscafe.com

Luma Bar and Eatery

The menu at Luma blends Mediterranean and California influences, with several options for plant-based diners. Tempura green beans come with scallion-sesame dressing, while a farro bowl pairs feta with garden greens, fig balsamic and Sherry vinaigrette. Larger dishes include a quinoa and chickpea veggie burger, agnolotti with lemon ricotta and peas, and a Margherita flatbread with the option of cashew cheese. The coconut creme brulee, served with Meyer lemon and pineapple sorbet, is a dessert worth saving room for. The drinks list includes local beer and wine, cocktails, and low- and no-alcohol options. 50 E. Washington St., Petaluma, 707-772-5037, lumaeatery.com

Lunchette

Salads and grain bowls are the focus at Lunchette, which also serves soup and pizza by the slice. Seasonal offerings have included a green vegetable soup and fall polenta with roasted mushrooms and delicata squash. For a more substantial vegan lunch, the tahini grain bowl combines organic brown rice, spinach, cucumber, spiced chickpeas, pickled cauliflower, rainbow carrots and roasted sweet potato. Date molasses, za’atar and tahini dressing bring the ingredients together. The bakery case includes plant-based chocolate brownies, tahini miso cookies and gluten-free carrot cake muffins. 25 Fourth St., Petaluma, 707-241-7443, lunchettepetaluma.com

Wild Goat Bistro

This European-style bistro inside the historic Great Petaluma Mill serves California-American cuisine and wood-fired pizzas, with a range of vegan and gluten-free choices. The vegan quinoa-sweet potato cakes offer an alternative to traditional crab cakes. They’re served with a Brussels sprouts slaw, lemon tahini, roasted red pepper sauce and cashew cream. The vegan shepherd’s pie combines roasted Italian fennel sausage with peas, carrots and mushrooms, topped with mashed potatoes. For pizza, The Pearl comes with plant-based mozzarella, basil, pepperoncini, beech mushrooms, caramelized pearl onions and savory vegan fennel sausage. 6 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-658-1156, wildgoatbistro.com

The Local

This Petaluma sandwich shop was once easy to overlook inside the Active Wellness Center at 1201 Redwood Way. It has since expanded with a second location in the Plaza North Shopping Center. The menu is relatively small, emphasizing locally sourced ingredients and carefully assembled sandwiches. The vegan Helen Putnam layers artichoke hearts, carrots, avocado, pickles, red onion, pickled ginger, roasted beet hummus and local greens on housemade focaccia. Other choices include a seasonal banh mi and the Russian River, with grilled eggplant, roasted red pepper, arugula, goat cheese, chimichurri and lemon aioli. Salads, rice bowls and smoothies round out the menu. 229 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma, 707-981-7100, thelocalpetaluma.com

Pho Sonoma

This restaurant’s vegan menu includes several dishes that draw on traditional Vietnamese flavors. The vegan lemongrass noodle soup is a good choice for anyone craving pho. It comes with mixed vegetables, rice noodles and soft fried tofu in a spicy lemongrass broth. Vegan spring rolls, filled with tofu, lettuce, bean sprouts, vermicelli and mint, are served with peanut sauce. Other options include curry tofu with mixed vegetables and simmer-fried eggplant and green beans with Thai basil in vegan oyster sauce, rich in garlic and umami. 140 Second St., Suite 120, Petaluma, 707-762-6888, phosonoma.com

Healdsburg

Little Saint

This upscale, farm-to-table restaurant takes a creative approach to plant-based cooking. Its menu includes a seitan- and beet-based burger and hearth-oven potatoes with rosemary-garlic aioli. Brunch offerings have included seasonal quiche and breakfast tacos with scrambled tofu and Fresno chile cashew crema. Dinner is geared toward sharing — start with housemade focaccia and a trio of dips: smoked carrot, beet hummus and cultured cashew. Seasonal lasagna layers vegetables such as leeks, squash and Bodega Red potatoes with herbed ricotta and bay-infused béchamel. Fruit tarts and housemade ice cream provide a changing selection of desserts. 25 North St., Healdsburg, 707-433-8207, littlesainthealdsburg.com

Plank Coffee

Plank Coffee offers a variety of vegetarian and vegan options, including plant-based sandwiches and several milk alternatives for coffee drinks. You can order breakfast sandwiches on croissants, housemade biscuits or bagels, with egg, dairy or vegan cheese, plus either smoky tempeh bacon or a Beyond Meat sausage patty. The mushroom sandwich is a particularly savory option, with braised greens, melted provolone or a vegan alternative, and cremini mushrooms sautéed with garlic, onion, tamari, thyme, and Bragg’s Liquid Aminos. It comes on toasted ciabatta. The pastry selection includes a vegan apricot-pecan bran muffin and an orange cake with a citrus glaze. 175 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg, 707-395-0572, and 227 N. Cloverdale Blvd., Cloverdale, 707-894-6187, plankcoffee.com

The Taste of Tea

This family-owned tea room serves Japanese tea and comfort food, including several satisfying vegetarian dishes. Its miso ramen is a signature dish, especially welcome on a chilly autumn day. The vegan version features a ginger-seasoned miso kombu broth with soft tofu, shredded nori, bamboo shoots, green onions and sprouts. For something other than soup, try the nameshi onigiri, rice balls wrapped in nori, or the hijiki don, a bowl of white rice topped with hijiki seaweed salad and half a shoyu-marinated egg. Dessert options include matcha ice cream and yuzu sorbet. The tea list includes more than 80 varieties, prepared by the restaurant’s tea docents. 109 North St., Healdsburg, 707-431-1995, thetasteoftea.com

Carmella

This plant-based juice shop, in the former Nectary space on Center Street, specializes in cold-pressed juices, smoothies, salads, toasts, parfaits and specialty lattes. Its Big Red juice combines beet, lemon, pineapple, coconut water, hibiscus tea, green apple and chia seeds. The Midnight Maca smoothie gets its deep blue color from spirulina and combines maca, dates, banana, almond butter and cashew milk. Salads change with the seasons: One popular option, the Cool Beans, pairs lentils, housemade hummus, sprouted mung beans, pickled red onions, crisp root vegetables and fermented cucumbers with greens, herbed yogurt dressing and quinoa crisps. Housemade pickles, whipped hummus, toast and herbed almond cheese are also available. 312 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-385-4657, carmellacarmella.com

Sebastopol

Cozy Plum Bistro

Burgers, burritos, nachos and macaroni and cheese are among the familiar comfort foods on the menu at this all-plant-based restaurant. Its planned closure this month, after more than six years in business, makes a visit especially timely.

The carne asada burrito combines soy-based carne asada with black beans, Spanish rice, crispy fried onions, avocado, salsa roja and chipotle aioli. The Philly cheesesteak, a plant-based take on the East Coast classic, uses gluten-based steak strips, bell peppers, onions and smoky cheddar sauce on a toasted French roll. The burgers feature a house blend of soy, pea and rice proteins, topped with Cozy sauce, pickles, tomato, onion and lettuce on a potato bun. 6970 McKinley St., Sebastopol, 707-823-3333, cozyplum.com

Fern Bar

This chic Sebastopol restaurant serves a range of vegan and vegetarian dishes, along with gluten-free and celiac-safe choices. The falafel plate is made for sharing, with dukkah-seasoned patties, cherry tomatoes, and Nardello peppertahina. The Umami Bomb, a vegan and celiac-safe dish, combines crispy rice with broccoli, mushrooms, shiitake cream, balsamic and nutritional yeast. For dessert, the warm churros are vegetarian and come coated in cinnamon sugar with apple butter. 6780 Depot St., Suite 120, Sebastopol, 707-861-9603, fernbar.com

La Bodega Kitchen

This entirely meat-free restaurant combines casual, rustic surroundings with a more elaborate approach to plant-based cooking. The saffron and rose petal arancini are a highlight: three fried Carnaroli rice balls made with Miyoko’s mozzarella and Forager Project Parmesan, served in marinara sauce. The lasagna Bolognese replaces traditional meat sauce with mushroom ragu, Beyond Meat Italian sausage and Impossible beef, topped with grated local cheese. Desserts include hazelnut tiramisu and chocolate ganache nut torte, both of which demonstrate how well plant-based ingredients can work in classic sweets. 2295 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-1832, sonomawineshop.com

Muir’s Tea Room

This English- and Scottish-style tea house has one of the county’s largest selections of vegan baked goods. Its tea service menus also include fully plant-based plates. The baking case features seasonal and year-round pies, tarts, cakes, cookies, muffins, scones, brownies and cupcakes. Even the double chocolate brownie and lemon cream pie are vegan. Savory choices include finger sandwiches, mushroom tarts, plant-based sausage rolls and seasonal pasties. 330 S. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-634-6143, muirstearoomandcafe.com

The Wild Poppy Cafe

What began as a small roadside cafe has grown into a west county fixture, with a second cafe and marketplace recently opening in The Barlow. The new location carries familiar dishes, including beans and greens served with housemade focaccia and vegan Cosmic Nachos topped with black bean puree, cashew crema, pepita chimichurri and cosmic queso. Other options include a vegan kale Caesar, tofu tacos and huevos rancheros with cornmeal-fried tofu. All menu items can be made gluten-free. 9890 Bodega Highway and 6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol, thewildpoppycafe.com

Viva Mexicana

While vegetable burritos are common at taquerias, Viva Mexicana devotes an entire menu page to vegan dishes. The Very Vegan Burrito is filled with Spanish rice, black beans, organic tofu, salsa verde and mango salsa, all wrapped in a Roma tomato tortilla. Another standout is the butternut squash enchilada: two corn tortillas filled with squash and served with roasted tomato-chipotle salsa, lettuce, avocado, cilantro, Spanish rice and refried beans. The menu also includes vegan nachos, tacos, soups, tamales, quesadillas and desserts. Bonus: From 4-8 p.m. daily, the restaurant adds another dimension to its menu with Persian Nights, featuring plant-basedIranian dishes inspired by the cooking owner Sima Mohamadian grew up with. 841 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-823-5555, vivamexicana.com

Sonoma

Spread Kitchen

This Lebanese-inspired restaurant in Boyes Hot Springs serves an assortment of richly seasoned plant-based dishes. Start with the cold mezze plate, with hummus, muhammara, baba ghanoush or labneh, plus pita, crudités, and housemade pickles. Other vegan options include roasted beet fattoush, falafel and cauliflower lavash wraps, and saffron rice bowls with vegetables, hummus and quinoa tabbouleh. The restaurant’s popular dirty fries are also available vegan. They’re seasoned with za’atar and topped with green tahini, toum garlic sauce, pickled onion and herbs. For dessert, the tahini brownie is both vegan and gluten-free. 18375 Highway 12, Sonoma, 707-721-1256, spreadkitchensonoma.com

Sunflower Caffe

Nearly half the menu at Sunflower Caffé is vegetarian-friendly, with meatless versions of brunch staples and several vegan options. The avocado toast is a standout, topped with watermelon radish, snap peas, a soft-boiled egg and feta on multigrain bread. For a sweeter breakfast, there’s vegan coconut chia pudding with granola, raspberries, toasted coconut and passion fruit sauce. The spiced chickpea and yam wrap combines sunflower-spiced chickpeas, herb-roasted yam, red onion, cucumber and tomato with coconut yogurt tzatziki. 421 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-6645, sonomasunflower.com

Valley

This Sonoma restaurant focuses on seasonal California cooking, with plant-based dishes appearing throughout the day. Weekend brunch includes the Valley mezze, served with flatbread, baba ghanoush, a soft-cooked egg, feta and vegetables. Lunch choices include a Hippie salad, fried green tomato sandwich and cold sesame noodles with tofu and chile oil. At dinner, cabbage with chile butter and lime and crispy rice with scallion-ginger sauce are among the options. 487 First W., Sonoma, 707-934-8403, valleybarandbottle.com

Guerneville

Boon Eat + Drink

Featured in local and national publications, chef Crista Luedtke’s modern bistro is a fixture of the Russian River dining scene. Its vegetarian polenta lasagna is one of the restaurant’s most popular dishes, layered with sautéed vegetables and ricotta, then served with spicy marinara and tender rainbow chard. The salads and shared plates also offer several meatless options. Burrata comes topped with roasted delicata squash, spiced nuts and Aleppo honey; a tri-colored beet salad pairs the beets with goat cheese and citrus vinaigrette. For vegan diners, a bowl of Italian butter beans with sautéed greens, seasonal vegetables and herbed pesto provides a more substantial choice. 16248 Main St., Guerneville, 707-869-0780, eatatboon.com

title: ReLeaf Petaluma’s Mission To Plant 750 Oaks All Starts With the Mighty Acorn
summary:
The Petaluma-based nonprofit collects hundreds of acorns every fall to grow new oak trees on bare city-owned land.

The post ReLeaf Petaluma’s Mission To Plant 750 Oaks All Starts With the Mighty Acorn appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The acorn: a mighty tree in a mini package. At a mere inch and a half or so in length, it contains all the information it needs to grow into a stately landmark, an ecosystem anchor, a branching, spreading, shading centenarian. Densely packed with nutrients, the acorn also includes an ample store of food for the young tree. Indigenous Californians shelled, ground, and leached these repositories of energy (and still do) — a time-consuming process producing a rich, life-sustaining mash.

Every fall, when acorns drop (beginning in early September, peaking in October, and continuing into November) ReLeaf Petaluma staff and volunteers collect large numbers of coast live oak, black oak, and valley oak acorns from Windsor to San Rafael for a different reason: to grow new trees on bare city-owned parcels.

“[Oaks are] a keystone species, so they’ll support the most biodiversity. Their roots will help hold onto soil and protect the waterways,” says Carolyn Lacerra, programs manager at ReLeaf, a nonprofit founded in 2020 to increase Petaluma’s urban tree canopy. The re-oaking program, just one of its many initiatives, was designed “to reclaim Petaluma open spaces that probably used to have oak trees on them, to re-establish those oaks,” Lacerra explains.

Once collected, the acorns are sprayed with alcohol to help prevent the spread of sudden oak death, says ReLeaf Petaluma tree consultant Kaitlin Magoon. Caused by a non-native pathogen, the disease has killed tens of millions of trees from Big Sur to southwest Oregon in recent decades. Sonoma County has more of the pathogen than any other county in California.

After the initial sterilization, “we give them a little float test to see which ones are viable,” says Lacerra. Viable acorns are sanitized again in a bleach-water solution, packed in plastic bags, and chilled for two to three months, mimicking the winter cold to provide a cue for them to later germinate. Once potted, ReLeaf’s oak saplings — maintained, for now, at an ersatz nursery at Lacerra’s house — are ready to plant that winter or the following fall. A smaller number of acorns go straight into the soil, sans cold stratification and pre-germination, at three to a hole to increase the odds of success.

The program got roughly 500 oaks in the ground during its first two years, with 250 remaining toward its goal of 750. Organizers expect to finish by the end of the coming fall-to-winter planting season. That’s quite an accomplishment, but Lacerra knows the true payoff lies years down the line: “When you go back and you look at these areas that we’ve planted, it’s just sort of amazing to think about what it’s going to look like 20 years from now, 30 years from now.”

title: Find Wine Deals and Free Corkage Nights at These Sonoma County Restaurants
summary:
Here are some of our favorite dining spots in Sonoma County for BYOB deals and complimentary corkage nights.

The post Find Wine Deals and Free Corkage Nights at These Sonoma County Restaurants appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Lately, it seems like restaurant wine pricing has gone through the roof. Why pay $18 for a single glass when you can bring your own bottle of Sonoma County wine and skip the corkage fee?

Here are some of our favorite dining spots for BYOB deals.

It’s hard to beat locals night at Baked on the River in Guerneville. On Thursdays, comfort food fans get a three-course dinner for $25 and free corkage. 16390 Fourth St., Guerneville. 707-865-6060, bakedontheriver.com

Petaluma’s Central Market is the place to be on Tuesdays, when the farm-to-fork restaurant offers complimentary corkage and 40% off wines by the bottle. 42 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-778-9900, centralmarketpetaluma.com

Every Monday, pay zero corkage and enjoy classic French fare in a romantic setting at La Gare French Restaurant in Santa Rosa. 208 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-528-4355, lagarerestaurant.com

Head for Glen Ellen Star every Wednesday for Neighborhood Night. That’s when diners can score two fresh and fabulous courses for $49, along with complimentary corkage. 13648 Arnold Drive, Glen Ellen, 707-343-1384, glenellenstar.com

Chef Charlie Palmer’s Dry Creek Kitchen and Folia Kitchen in Healdsburg waive the corkage fee for the first two bottles of BYO Sonoma County wines. Dry Creek Kitchen, 317 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-431-0330, drycreekkitchen.com. Folia Bar & Kitchen, 101 Dovetail Lane, Healdsburg, 707-723-2130, foliabarandkitchen.com

On Mondays, Stella offers free corkage on unlimited bottles to enjoy with the Kenwood restaurant’s exquisite, housemade pastas. 9049 Sonoma Highway, Kenwood, 707-801-8043, stellakenwood.com

Sonoma Wine Shop & La Bodega, a homey Sebastopol hub for elevated plant-based cuisine, never charges a corkage fee for diners who bring in a bottle from the on-site wine shop. 2295 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-1832, sonomawineshop.com

At The Madrona, known for its epic burger and gorgeous salads, corkage is on the house during lunch service Wednesday through Friday. 1001 Westside Road, Healdsburg, 707-395-6700, themadronahotel.com

Glen Ellen’s Poppy doesn’t technically offer free corkage, but the weeknight family-style meal is the next best thing. Get three courses, including wine, for $65 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays. 13690 Arnold Drive, Glen Ellen, 707-938-2130, poppyglenellen.com

Sugo Trattoria is a Petaluma go-to for fresh Italian food. It’s even more popular on Mondays, when diners can bring their own wine with zero corkage. 5 Petaluma Blvd. S., Suite B, Petaluma, 707-782-9298, sugotrattoria.com

This story was excerpted from our feature on Sonoma County Wineries Building a Brighter Future, originally published in the September/October 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: 8 Spooky Spots in Sonoma County
summary:
For Halloween or any day of the year, here are Sonoma County's most haunted places to visit — if you dare.

The post 8 Spooky Spots in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County has no shortage of ghost stories. Passed down through generations, local legends have also drawn attention from paranormal investigators and curious visitors.

One of the county’s best-known allegedly haunted destinations is the Fairmont Sonoma Mission Inn & Spa in Boyes Hot Springs. Historic Hotels of America, a program of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, recently named the resort to its annual list of the 25 most haunted hotels in the country. The property has appeared on the list every year since 2019.

According to Historic Hotels of America, the resort’s reported paranormal activity includes sightings of Victoria, an early European settler said to wander the grounds when fog rolls in from San Francisco Bay.

“Fairmont Sonoma Mission Inn & Spa in Sonoma, California, welcomes guests past and present, reflecting a belief that spirits linger where they were happiest,” the list states. “Victoria is said to have celebrated her wedding and many anniversaries at the resort.”

For those drawn to the macabre, here are eight places around Sonoma County with reputations for ghostly activity.

A note on the supernatural: The accounts that follow are based on local lore, reported sightings and paranormal investigations; they have not been independently verified. Some locations featured in the article are private property. Respect posted signs and do not trespass or disturb residents.

Sonoma

Fairmont Sonoma Mission Inn & Spa

Originally opened as the Boyes Hot Springs Hotel in 1902, the property sits on land where Indigenous Pomo, Miwok and Wappo peoples frequented the area’s healing mineral springs. Fire destroyed the hotel in 1923, and it reopened as the Sonoma Mission Inn in 1927.

Beyond the legend of Victoria, guests have reported unexplained phenomena, including flickering lights, slamming doors, running water and shadowy figures darting through hallways. The inn’s so-called Round Room is reputed to be its most haunted space. According to one unsubstantiated story, a jealous lover beheaded a guest in a bathtub there in the 1920s.

Visitors interested in the property’s history can join historic walking tours led by local historians on the second Sunday of each month. The tours offer a closer look at the resort’s past, whether participants encounter anything supernatural or not. The next tour is scheduled for Nov. 8.

100 Boyes Blvd., Sonoma, 707-938-9000, fairmont-sonoma.com

Sebastiani Theatre

Built in 1933, the historic Sebastiani Theatre near the Sonoma Plaza is allegedly home to a few benevolent spirits, including Barbara, a former stage manager who allegedly fell to her death from the catwalk above the stage.

Kelly, sometimes called Trixie, is a 16-year-old girl said to appear in the women’s restroom mirror wearing a 1920s-style yellow dress.

A more menacing presence, known as the Shadow Man, is said to haunt the balcony, where an alleged murder is part of the theater’s lore.

476 First St. E., Sonoma, 707-996-2020, sebastianitheatre.org

Buena Vista Winery

Buena Vista Winery dates back to 1857, but its ghost stories have become part of its modern mystique.

In a 2021 Sonoma Index-Tribune article, paranormal investigator Ellen MacFarlane of Napa Ghost Tours recounts a story about the winery’s cleaning crew, which allegedly quit one night during the Great Recession after seeing an apparition climb the tasting-room staircase.

MacFarlane’s team also reported hearing loud banging on the third floor, an otherwise empty warehouse space, likening the noise to “a herd of elephants.”

The team believes the winery may be haunted by an “insane woman” who lived in a nearby home for wayward women, as well as by Chinese laborers who reportedly died when a wine cave collapsed during its construction. According to the legend, the men’s cries for help can still be heard echoing through the winery.

18000 Old Winery Road, Sonoma, 800-926-1266, buenavistawinery.com

The Sonoma Plaza Ghost Walking Tour

For those who would rather hear ghost stories while exploring downtown, the Sonoma Plaza Ghost Walking Tour offers a guided introduction to the area’s haunted lore.

Ellen MacFarlane and Devin Sisk launched the Napa City Ghosts & Legends Walking Tour in 2014, followed by the Sonoma tour two years later. The walk visits sites around the plaza and draws on the region’s darker history, including violent battles and the enslavement and dispossession of Indigenous peoples.

Tours cost $30 per person, plus tax. Reservations and additional information are available online at napaghosts.com.

Meeting location: First Street East, Sonoma.

Petaluma

Phoenix Theater

Over the years, psychics, ghost hunters and exorcists have visited the Phoenix Theater in response to staff members’ and guests’ reports of paranormal activity. Longtime theater manager Tom Gaffey has recounted unexplained incidents, including calls apparently coming from the projection booth when no one was there.

One of the venue’s best-known stories involves a security guard working during a 1990s performance by the heavy metal band GWAR. After climbing down a ladder, the guard reportedly asked an employee, “Who’s that little kid back there in the exit?” According to the account, when no child could be found, the guard quit.

Gaffey has also said he saw the child, described as wearing 1920s-style clothing, on separate occasions.

201 Washington St., Petaluma, 707-762-3566, thephoenixtheater.com

Washoe House

The historic Washoe House, dating to the 1850s, has attracted its share of paranormal curiosity. According to a 2016 article in the Petaluma Argus-Courier, a five-person team from NorCal Paranormal Investigators examined the landmark and concluded that it was haunted.

The investigators used an electromagnetic field meter and photographed the building. One image allegedly showed two apparitions near a window: a balding man visible from the torso up and another figure wearing a cowboy hat.

2840 Roblar Road, Petaluma, 707-795-4544, thewashoehouse1859.com

Santa Rosa

Hotel La Rose

Built in 1907, Hotel La Rose is a historic fixture of downtown Santa Rosa’s Railroad Square. The property appeared in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1943 psychological thriller “Shadow of a Doubt,” though its ghost stories are rooted in local legend rather than the movie.

According to a 2017 Press Democrat article, hotel staff have reported paranormal activity in Room 42, where one family is said to have checked in and never left. A young boy named Daniel allegedly rides the elevators in search of his parents, while guests have reported flickering lights and elevator doors opening onto empty floors.

308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-579-3200, hotellarose.com

Bodega

Potter Schoolhouse

The historic Potter Schoolhouse in Bodega gained wider recognition as a filming location for Hitchcock’s 1963 horror film “The Birds.” It has also inspired stories of unexplained activity.

In a 2013 Press Democrat article, owner Leah Taylor described seeing a floating apparition surrounded by what she called a “silver aura.” She also recounted finding unusual grease stains on a chalkboard menu that appeared to resemble Calvin Keithly, one of the school’s first teachers, who died in 1876.

A separate Press Democrat article from the same year recounted a story from Taylor’s mother, Mary Taylor, who bought the building with her husband, Tom, in the 1960s. Mary reportedly heard an Irish woman wailing for her baby. Nearby, at St. Teresa of Avila Church, is the grave of Ellen Orr, who died in 1861, allegedly during childbirth. Taylor speculated that Orr might be the source of the cries.

The family also reported seeing a cradle rock on its own and hearing unexplained knocking and footsteps.

The Potter Schoolhouse is a private residence. Do not trespass or disturb the occupants. bodegaschool.com

The Press Democrat has also reported haunting legends associated with nearby properties, including the John McCrea House, the Franceschi House and The Casino Bar & Grill.

A grandson of former Casino owner Art Casini, who died in 1983, reportedly claimed that Casini’s spirit appeared near the pool table in the early morning hours.

The post 8 Spooky Spots in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Red Eye Barbecue Brings Texas-Style BBQ to Santa Rosa’s Epicenter
summary:
Bob Costarella trades his Saturday barbecue pop-ups for a 250-seat restaurant at Santa Rosa's Epicenter, serving Texas-style smoked meats, fried chicken and more.

The post Red Eye Barbecue Brings Texas-Style BBQ to Santa Rosa’s Epicenter appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Bob Costarella likes a big challenge: sweating through a summer flipping brisket in a Central Texas smokehouse, tackling regimented 75-day health challenges or opening a 250-seat restaurant in Santa Rosa.

At this point in his life, not much fazes him. Except, perhaps, frozen mozzarella sticks and chicken tenders. Those scare the living daylights out of him.

Sitting inside his new restaurant, Red Eye Barbecue at Epicenter, Costarella takes a brief breather after a weekend of nonstop service at the 130,000-square-foot entertainment and sports complex. There are the daily demands of running a restaurant, along with banquets, pizza parties and hours spent tending enormous smokers. Eighty-hour workweeks are nothing unusual as the restaurant finds its footing.

Then there are the steady requests from previous customers to bring back mozzarella sticks and chicken tenders from the previous restaurant’s menu.

For Costarella, food is his happy place. The leap from a tiny, Saturday-only barbecue pop-up to executive chef of a sprawling family entertainment complex that feeds hundreds of people for as many as 12 hours a day was more than a promotion. It was a great white shark-size bite he’s still trying to wrap his jaws around.

But this is a man who can persuade devoted brisket lovers to try beef cheeks — his specialty. A challenge is rarely reason enough to back down.

The backstory

Costarella arrived on the Sonoma County barbecue scene in late 2025, after spending a year apprenticing under famed pitmaster Lance Kirkpatrick at Stiles Switch BBQ in Austin, Texas. In the barbecue world, a mentor can matter almost as much as the meat on the smoker, with techniques and secrets passed down through generations.

Kirkpatrick trained under the late Bobby Mueller, a James Beard Award winner whose Louie Mueller Barbecue is often called the “Cathedral of Smoke.” In a sense, Costarella is carrying on a tradition of Texas barbecue royalty.

During his year of training, nearly three months passed before Kirkpatrick stopped readjusting every log Costarella placed on the fire. Under a tin roof, freezing some mornings and sweating through others, Costarella learned to cook by touch and instinct. He estimates he tended about 15,000 briskets.

He brought that experience to Sonoma County, where over six months, he built a following through Saturday pop-ups at Sazon Peruvian Cuisine & Deli in Roseland. His cooking married Texas-style rubs and deeply smoked meats with California influences: serious barbecue that did not feel bound by Texas tradition.

His Roseland run ended this spring, leaving him open to something new. That’s when the owners of Epicenter came calling.

From the frying pan into the fire

In June, the owners of Epicenter approached Costarella about taking over the large, outdated restaurant at the Piner Road sports and entertainment complex. They had found him on Yelp, read the positive reviews and reached out. Within weeks, he had abandoned plans for his own barbecue trailer and taken over the former Victory House restaurant.

The new job is a far cry from the one-man operation that attracted hardcore barbecue fans who understood that when the brisket ran out, it ran out.

At Epicenter, the clientele ranges from birthday parties and soccer teams to sports fans watching the dozens of flickering televisions surrounding the main dining room. This is not the place for a romantic evening unless you don’t mind a little distraction. The restaurant is busy, loud and expected to satisfy a wide range of appetites.

For nearly a decade, the former Victory House menu centered on pub standards: burgers, pasta, pizza, flatbreads and fish tacos. The restaurant had its loyal customers, and Costarella knows that some dishes are nonnegotiable. Pretzel bites with cheese and chicken tenders, for example, are coming back.

Flexibility is essential. Sometimes you have to serve tenders. Costarella, however, is doing it his way.

He has overhauled the kitchen, replacing frozen and prepackaged products with scratch-made sauces, sides and desserts. The smokers fire up at 6 a.m., turning out hundreds of pounds of meat over oak and applewood. And he is bringing serious cooking techniques to a menu that must also appeal to kids fresh off the baseball field.

“I’m not just a barbecue guy. I like to cook a lot more than barbecue,” he said. “I don’t really like to define myself.”

Still, feeding hundreds of people, many of whom care more about Warrior games than the perfect bark on a brisket, has been a reality check. Costarella calls it the most stressful thing he has ever done.

A month into the job, he has recalibrated, regrouped and is almost ready to give himself a weekend off. Almost.

Learning to let go

Costarella’s biggest adjustment has been learning to run a kitchen in which he can’t do everything himself.

“I haven’t had a boss in 17 years,” he said.

Although he has worked in plenty of kitchens, he has never been a sous chef. The organizational demands of a large restaurant have made management a crash course in its own right.

Building a team, largely from the existing kitchen staff, has become an unexpected source of satisfaction. He is teaching cooks everything from knife skills to the finer points of making crème anglaise.

As his team grows more confident, Costarella can spend less time worrying about the daily grind and more time dreaming up what comes next. He’s already thinking about a bigger menu, more ambitious specials and dishes that go well beyond Texas barbecue.

“I want this to become a culinary epicenter,” he said. “Your dreams should scare the hell out of you, and if not, you’re not reaching far enough.”

Best bets

Red Eye Barbecue offers a limited smoked-meat menu on Mondays and Tuesdays. Beef and pork ribs, pork belly, brisket and half chickens aren’t available on those days, but beef cheeks, sausage, turkey, and wings remain on the menu. Burgers, sandwiches, sides and desserts are available all week.

Beef and pork ribs: Costarella’s signature offerings are smoked over applewood from a Martinelli orchard and vineyard, proof that even barbecue can have terroir in Sonoma County. The beef ribs get a proprietary Red Eye spice rub. At $44 a pound, the beef is the standout, though both versions deliver. A full rack of pork ribs costs $48.

Beef cheeks, $24: Costarella’s alternative to brisket, sometimes called “baby brisket,” comes from the cow’s cheek, a cut prized for its tenderness and collagen-rich texture after a long, slow bath. Bathed in beef tallow, the meat is extraordinarily rich. A drizzle of green salsa and a scattering of garlic chips, soaked in milk before frying, cut through the intensity. It’s richer than an oligarch, but sometimes that’s exactly what you want. Consider sharing.

Fried chicken sandwich, $18: A perfectly crispy chicken thigh that’s not too thick or thin gets just the right amount of breading. Order it hot or mild, but don’t skip the bird sauce, a blend of mayonnaise, ketchup, pickle juice, brown sugar and a whole lot of spices.

Smoked burger, $19: Angus beef goes into the smoker and emerges with a satisfying depth of flavor. The half-pound patty stays juicy beneath Thousand Island-style sauce and American cheese, all tucked into a brioche bun.

Sides and shares, $5-14: Costarella has raised the bar with additions including chips and queso, salads, fried Oaxaca cheese and fries cooked in beef tallow. All are worth ordering. If you have room for only a few, make them the roasted potato salad with black truffle mayo, macaroni and cheese with garlic cornflakes, cowboy lentils and cheddar cornbread with roasted onion butter.

Wings, $11-20: These wings get the full treatment: a dry rub followed by a coating of Buffalo sauce made with miso paste and butter. Score.

Banana pudding, $10: More custard than pudding, this dessert layers banana compote, cornmeal butter cookie crumbles, whipped cream and espresso powder. It’s a world away from the artificial yellow stuff that comes from a box, and you can keep your Nilla wafers.

Red Eye Barbecue is at 3215 Coffey Lane, Santa Rosa. 707-757-9041, redeyebarbecue.com. Open noon to 10 p.m. Monday through Thursday; noon to midnight Friday; 11 a.m. to midnight Saturday; and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sunday.
